sessions.title: AI Won’t Replace Technical Writers - It’s Changing How We Work
sessions.description:
Artificial Intelligence has rapidly become part of the technical writing workflow. From generating outlines and improving grammar to creating drafts and summarizing complex information, AI tools are changing how documentation is created.

But while these tools can increase speed and productivity, they also introduce new challenges such as inaccuracies, missing context, and content that appears correct but fails in real-world use.

This talk explores the evolving relationship between AI and technical writing through practical examples and real-world experiences.

Attendees will learn where AI can effectively support technical writers, where human expertise remains essential, and how writers can use AI as a collaborative tool rather than viewing it as a replacement.

The session will cover:

- Practical ways AI can assist documentation workflows
- Common limitations and risks of AI-generated content
- Why human judgment, testing, and audience understanding still matter
- Strategies for integrating AI while maintaining quality and trust

Participants will leave with a balanced perspective on AI and a clearer understanding of how technical writers can adapt and grow alongside emerging technologies.

sessions.title: Navigating Documentation Challenges: Success Stories from the OpenMRS Wiki Revamp Project
sessions.description:
If you've seen or used a wiki and immediately wished you hadn't, you already know the feeling I want to talk about.

That was the OpenMRS Wiki when I first got my hands on it.

After years of contributions from a global community that spread across hundreds of pages, the wiki had lost structure.

You had outdated guides sitting next to current ones, and any information you needed was buried three clicks deep under information you didn't.

For four months, I led the project to fix it.

And what I want to share at WTD Kenya is what that work actually looked like, because "we revamped the wiki" makes it sound a lot cleaner than it was.

This talk walks through the maze-like pattern of large-scale documentation work. My talk aims to answer questions like:

- How do you audit content when there's too much of it to read in one sitting?

- How do you restructure an Information Architecture that an entire community has spent years building muscle memory around?

- How do you make decisions about what stays, what goes, and what gets rewritten without breaking the trust of contributors scattered across every time zone?

And maybe the hardest question of all: how do you build something that doesn't fall right back into chaos the moment you step away?

I'll share the things that worked, the things that didn't, and the small choices that turned out to matter way more than I expected.

The goal isn't to hand anyone a perfect playbook, because there isn't one. It's to give you a real look at what it takes to untangle documentation at scale, so when you face your own version of this — and if you work in docs long enough, you will — you'll have some patterns to reach for.

sessions.title: Documenting an AI That Sees the Physical World: Building a CI/CD Pipeline for Foundation Model Docs
sessions.description:
AI products break documentation faster than any software category before them. Model behaviour shifts between releases, SDK surface areas expand weekly, and code examples that worked on Monday return different outputs by Friday. For developer-facing AI platforms, "docs as code" stops being a nice-to-have and becomes the only way to keep pace.
In this talk, I'll walk through how I built an end-to-end documentation CI/CD pipeline for a physical AI foundation model platform, one that ingests multimodal sensor data through a Python SDK and REST API. Using Mintlify, GitHub Actions, and Vale, we layered validation so documentation shipped with the same rigour as the product: prose linting tuned to our voice, broken link detection across internal and external references, code sample validation so examples never went stale, and preview deployments that let engineers review docs the same way they review pull requests.
I'll share what didn't work the first time: overly strict Vale rules that turned every PR into a fight, link checkers that flagged false positives until we tuned them, and the cultural work of getting engineers to actually engage with doc reviews.
Attendees will leave with a concrete blueprint: which checks to add first, how to layer them without slowing contributors down, and how to keep AI documentation honest when the underlying model keeps moving.
You'll leave with:

A staged checklist of doc CI/CD validations ranked by ROI
Vale + Mintlify configuration patterns specific to AI/ML platform docs
GitHub Actions workflows for docs that won't annoy your engineers
How to keep code examples valid against a moving model target

sessions.title: Understand LLMs and RAG basics to write better product content
sessions.description:
We'll solve this scenario:

You content leadership is questioning why customers sometimes receive inaccurate responses from external AI search tools like Google or Bing AI Overview when interacting with your content.

As a technical writer, you need to understand how AI interprets and uses product documentation so you can structure your content in a way that improves accurate retrieval, reduces hallucinations, and ensures your documentation remains a reliable source—without requiring you to become a developer.

sessions.description:

We will provide a hands-on demonstration where we migrate a sample application deployed on Google App Engine to Docker containers and then deploy them to Cloud Run. This will help us understand how proper documentation can solve many problems related to documentation itself, including reproducibility.

By the end of this presentation, you will have a better understanding of documenting Docker workflows and the best practices for writing a migration guide.

sessions.title: The 5-Minute README Fix: Small Changes, Big Impact
sessions.description:
Every open‑source project starts with a README — but most READMEs are written for people who already understand the project. What about the newcomer?

In this lightning talk, I’ll show you three fixes you can make in five minutes or less that turn a confusing README into a welcoming, usable front door. No heavy rewrites. No perfect prose. Just small, human actions: adding a clear “what this does” first line, writing a setup step a beginner could follow, and including one obvious place to ask for help.

I’ve mentored dozens of students and new contributors. The biggest barrier is never the code — it’s the documentation that assumes too much. Let’s change that together.

sessions.title: The APT Approach to Documentation: Consistency Over CV Padding
sessions.description:
In cybersecurity, an APT — Advanced Persistent Threat — isn’t flashy. It doesn’t rush. It shows up consistently, learns the terrain, and plays a long game most defenders don’t have the patience for.

What if documentarians adopted the same long-game mindset? Not for breaching networks, but for building documentation that outlasts sprint cycles, job hops, and the temptation to copy-paste from Western templates.

This talk reimagines the APT as a metaphor for the kind of technical communicator Africa needs: patient, adaptive, vision-driven, and committed to building something real — not just a CV.

I’ll share how shifting from “building a CV” to “building a dream” changed my own work, from red team tools to youth empowerment, and why the best documentation comes from consistent, self-respecting creation, not mimicry. Attendees will leave with a mental model for long-term documentation impact that has nothing to do with tools and everything to do with identity.

sessions.title: How Cursor Uses Documentation to Build Better AI Coding Workflows
sessions.description:
AI coding tools are changing how we write software — but I’ve learned that behind every great AI-generated response is great documentation.

In this lightning talk, I’ll share how I use Cursor’s documentation indexing and retrieval workflows to build faster and more accurate AI-assisted development experiences. I’ll walk through how modern AI coding tools rely on documentation retrieval, embeddings, and contextual search to reduce hallucinations and generate better code suggestions.

Using practical demos and real-world workflows from my experience as a software engineer and Cursor Regional Lead for Africa, I’ll show how documentation is becoming a core part of the AI development stack — not just something written after the code is complete.

In this session, I’ll cover:

How I use Cursor to index and retrieve documentation
Why AI coding assistants depend on high-quality documentation
How I structure documentation for better AI workflows
Common mistakes I’ve seen with AI-generated documentation
How developers and technical writers can collaborate better in AI-native teams

Whether you are a developer, technical writer, DevRel engineer, or documentation enthusiast, I hope this session gives you practical insight into the future of documentation in the age of AI-assisted software development.

Key Takeaway:
I believe AI coding assistants are only as good as the documentation they can retrieve.

sessions.title: Code is Cheap, Context is Expensive: Docs that Survive the FinTech Fire
sessions.description:
In high-stakes environments—like USSD banking cores, payment gateways, and blockchain infrastructure—the most dangerous bug isn't a syntax error; it's ambiguity. When a mission-critical system fails at 3:00 AM, "pretty" documentation is useless. You need a flight manual.

Most documentation is written for the "Happy Path"—explaining how things work when everything is fine. This session flips the script. Drawing from years of building high-concurrency backend systems in Nairobi’s FinTech ecosystem, I will argue that documentation is a safety-critical engineering component, not a post-project chore.

We will move past the "how-to" and dive into Operational Documentation: the art of writing for resilience, clarity under pressure, and absolute accountability.
Key Takeaways:

    The Zero-Context Principle: How to document for the "paged" developer who has zero mental context and a ticking SLA clock.

    Documentation as a Compiler Constraint: Using Go/Rust schemas and Protobufs to ensure your docs are technically incapable of lying.

    The QRH Framework: Why your READMEs should look more like Aviation Quick Reference Handbooks and less like blog posts.

    Failure-Mode First: Shifting focus from "How to start" to "How it breaks" to drastically reduce Mean Time to Recovery (MTTR).

    The AI Agent Ready-Room: Structuring your docs so that the next generation of autonomous coding agents can actually help you fix bugs instead of hallucinating them.

sessions.title: Cultivating AI Literacy: Making Tech Documentation Inclusive for All Communities
sessions.description:
As artificial intelligence continues to reshape our digital landscape, the gap between complex technical documentation and grass-roots community understanding widens. This interactive workshop focuses on strategies for breaking down advanced AI concepts and technical workflows into highly accessible, community-friendly documentation.
Participants will explore practical frameworks for designing inclusive manuals, leveraging localized examples, and ensuring that digital literacy materials are structured to empower diverse audiences, regardless of their technical background.

sessions.title: Docs in the Real World: Platforms, AI, and the Cost of Getting It Right
sessions.description:
Behind every great documentation site is a series of hard decisions — and a few expensive lessons. This session draws from hands-on experience owning and maintaining API and platform documentation, including the realities of evaluating, adopting, and sometimes reconsidering third-party docs platforms as they evolve, reprice, and reshape themselves around AI.
We'll explore three threads that are increasingly intertwined in modern documentation work: the rise of AI tooling (MCP servers, markdown-native workflows, and what it means when your docs platform leans into LLM integrations); the challenge of internationalization and what "inclusive docs" actually costs in practice; and the quieter, often underappreciated work of building docs-as-code pipelines that actually get engineers to contribute.
Whether you're a seasoned technical writer navigating platform migrations, a developer who has ever been intimidated opening an API reference for the first time, or someone just starting out and weighing your tooling options; this session offers honest perspective on the trade-offs, the wins, and what to watch out for.

sessions.title: The Docs We Don't Call Documentation
sessions.description:
For the longest time, if you had asked me what documentation was, I would have pointed you to API docs, a README perhaps or a technical manual.

After all, whenever people in tech said "document it," that's what I imagined they meant.

Then I started noticing something interesting.

The product manager maintained a PRD that everyone referenced before making decisions. The ops team had a Notion workspace explaining how things actually got done. Someone created an onboarding guide for themselves, and months later it had become required reading for every new hire.

None of these people called themselves technical writers.

Yet they were all documenting.

That's when I realized that some of the most important documentation in our organizations isn't even called documentation.

This talk explores the hidden documentation that powers collaboration every day. We'll uncover how knowledge is captured, shared, and preserved by people in roles that don't traditionally identify as "documentation roles."

By broadening our understanding of documentation, we can create more inclusive documentation cultures where everyone sees themselves as contributors to shared knowledge rather than documentation being the responsibility of a single team or individual.

Whether you're a developer, designer, product manager,  or someone who's been told to document their work, this session will help you recognize the documentation already happening around you and understand why it matters.

Key Takeaways
- Why documentation is not just a developer or technical writer responsibility.
- How to recognize the documentation already happening within your team, even if no one calls it documentation
- Simple ways to start capturing processes, decisions, and knowledge regardless of your role or technical background
- How shared documentation reduces the "ask me every time" problem and strengthens collaboration
- Lightweight tools and approaches that non-coding professionals can use to document effectively

sessions.title: Multilingual docs without losing your mind (or your meaning)
sessions.description: Kenya alone has 68 languages. How do you build localisation workflows that scale, maintain quality across translations, and resist the temptation to just run everything through Google Translate and call it done?

sessions.title: Beyond the Notebook: Architecting Organizational Memory for ML Teams
sessions.description:
People often say machine learning is all about building models, but really, it’s more about wrangling knowledge. If you’ve worked on a real ML project, you know how easy it is for key decisions to disappear—one day you’re discussing why a model needs a tweak, and by next week, the reasoning is buried in an old teams thread or lost in a passing comment. Notebooks fill up, messages scatter, crucial context fades away. So teams end up with "documentation debt": a growing pile of missing explanations that triples the time it takes to onboard someone new, leads to teams re-running the same failed experiments, and quietly erodes true collaboration.

This talk argues we need to ditch our passive approach to ML documentation. Treating documentation as an afterthought hasn’t worked. Instead, what if teams deliberately designed collaboration right into their ML workflows? Imagine systems that don’t just log numbers—they record why you tried a new architecture, what trade-offs you debated, or how you handled weird data artifacts.

We will introduce a practical framework built around three components: structured decision logs, experiment tracking with context, and data documentation that preserves meaning and lineage. We will also explore how AI tools can help translate technical experiment results into clear summaries for both engineers and non-technical stakeholders.

When you walk out of this talk, you’ll have a practical blueprint for running and improving collaboration, onboarding, and long-term maintainability in ML projects.

sessions.title: From Static Docs to Executables: Building Replayable and Verifiable Documentation Workflows
sessions.description:
Technical documentation has evolved significantly through the docs-as-code movement. We version documentation, review it in pull requests, and publish it through CI/CD pipelines.

But one major problem still remains:

Most technical documentation is static, while the systems it describes are dynamic and changing with every turn of deployment.

As a result, UI walkthroughs drift, screenshots become outdated, tutorials silently break and quick starts fail. Browser demos depend on fragile manual steps and endless re-recording.

In this talk, I’ll introduce slides-tape, a Markdown-first orchestration engine for executable technical content. slides-tape combines presentations, browser automation, terminal execution, narration, and recording into a unified workflow that allows documentation and demos to become replayable, verifiable, and reproducible.

We’ll explore:

* how browser automation can power executable tutorials
* how deterministic replay changes technical storytelling
* how “docs-as-test” workflows can continuously validate onboarding guides and demos
* how Markdown can evolve from static content into executable developer experiences

The session will include live examples of browser-driven documentation flows, automated demo playback, and verification pipelines that ensure tutorials continue working as products evolve.

sessions.title: From Dead Docs to Searchable Knowledge
sessions.description: Most engineering teams already have documentation in Notion pages, Google Docs, GitHub READMEs and internal wikis. The challenge is that finding the right information quickly is often harder than writing it again or asking someone on the team. This session explores how Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) can transform scattered internal documentation into searchable, context-aware knowledge systems that developers actually use.

sessions.title: Tailoring Open source contribution for career transitions
sessions.description:
Breaking into tech can feel intimidating. 
From the outside, it often looks like a closed club with its own language, rules, and insiders. But here’s the reality: tech communities are the bridge that transforms outsiders into insiders and they are open to anyone willing to engage.
